title.en: Ataorupagui and Cusicayo: The Canari Brothers After the Flood
title.zh: 阿陶魯帕瓜伊與庫西卡約:洪水後的卡尼亞里兄弟

region.en: Mountain of Guasano, near Tumipampa, Quito (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基多通米潘帕附近的瓜薩諾山(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 6, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: In the time of the deluge called unu pachacuti there was a mountain named Guasano in the province of Quito, near the town of Tumipampa, which the natives still point out. Up this mountain went two of the Canaris named Ataorupagui and Cusicayo; as the waters increased the mountain kept rising and keeping above them, so that it was never covered by the flood. When the waters abated the two brothers began to sow. One day, returning to their hut, they found small loaves of bread and a jar of chicha they had not prepared; the next day the same thing happened. They hid themselves to spy out the bringers of their food, and saw two Canari women preparing the victuals. The men tried to seize them, but the women escaped; the brothers, seeing their mistake in molesting those who had done them so much good, prayed to Viracocha for pardon, entreating him to let the women return. The Creator granted their petition: the women came back, saying 'The Creator has thought it well that we should return to you, lest you should die of hunger.' One brother had connexion with one of the women; the elder brother was drowned in a lake near by, and the survivor married one of the women, with the other as concubine. By them he had ten sons who formed two lineages of five each, called Hanansaya (the upper party) and Hurinsaya (the lower party), from whom all the Canaris that now exist are descended.
summary.zh: 在名為「烏努-帕查庫提」的洪水時代,基多省通米潘帕鎮附近有一座瓜薩諾山,土人至今猶能指認。卡尼亞里兄弟二人——阿陶魯帕瓜伊與庫西卡約——登上此山;水漲山亦漲,始終浮於洪水之上,兄弟遂得倖存。水退之後,二人開始耕種。一日勞作歸來,見茅屋中備有麵餅與一罐奇恰酒,並非他們所置;次日亦然。二人藏匿窺探,見兩名卡尼亞里女子在備餐。他們撲上捉拿,女子卻逃脫。兄弟懊悔錯怪了善待自己的人,遂向維拉科查祈罪,求女子歸來。造物主允其所請;女子歸來說:「造物主命我們回到你們身邊,免得你們餓死。」其一兄與一女子結合;兄長在近旁湖中溺亡,倖存者娶其一女,以另一女為妾。二女共生十子,分為每支五人的兩個世系:上支「哈南薩亞」與下支「烏林薩亞」——今日所有卡尼亞里人皆出其後。

sensitivity.note: Sarmiento's Canari flood variant; Markham's note observes Molina's macaw version is the same story differently told - recorded as a named variant.

passages.text: They say that in the time of the deluge called unu pachacuti there was a mountain named Guasano in the province of Quito and near a town called Tumipampa. The natives still point it out. Up this mountain went two of the Canaris named Ataorupagui and Cusicayo. As the waters increased the mountain kept rising and keeping above them in such a way that it was never covered by the waters of the flood. In this way the two Canaris escaped. These two, who were brothers, when the waters abated after the flood, began to sow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 6 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day when they had been at work, on returning to their hut, they found in it some small loaves of bread, and a jar of chicha, which is the beverage used in this country in place of wine, made of boiled maize. They did not know who had brought it, but they gave thanks to the Creator, eating and drinking of that provision. Next day the same thing happened. As they marvelled at this mystery, they were anxious to find out who brought the meals. So one day they hid themselves, to spy out the bringers of their food. While they were watching they saw two Canari women preparing the victuals and putting them in the accustomed place. When about to depart the men tried to seize them, but they evaded their would-be captors and escaped.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 6 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Canaris, seeing the mistake they had made in molesting those who had done them so much good, became sad and prayed to Viracocha for pardon for their sins, entreating him to let the women come back and give them the accustomed meals. The Creator granted their petition. The women came back and said to the Canaris: 'The Creator has thought it well that we should return to you, lest you should die of hunger.' They brought them food. Then there was friendship between the women and the Canari brothers, and one of the Canari brothers had connexion with one of the women. Then, as the elder brother was drowned in a lake which was near, the survivor married one of the women, and had the other as a concubine. By them he had ten sons who formed two lineages of five each, and increasing in numbers they called one Hanansaya which is the same as to say the upper party, and the other Hurinsaya, or the lower party. From these all the Canaris that now exist are descended.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 6 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)

title.en: The Moon Was Brighter: Ashes Thrown on Her Face
title.zh: 月本更明:一把爐灰毀其容

region.en: Lake Titicaca, island of Titicaca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 的的喀喀湖太陽島(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 7, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Viracocha went with his servants to a great lake in the Collao, in which there is an island called Titicaca, the meaning being 'the rock of lead'. Viracocha went to this island, and presently ordered that the sun, moon, and stars should come forth, and be set in the heavens to give light to the world, and it was so. They say that the moon was created brighter than the sun, which made the sun jealous at the time when they rose into the sky. So the sun threw over the moon's face a handful of ashes, which gave it the shaded colour it now presents.
summary.zh: 維拉科查攜僕從來到科利亞奧大湖,湖中有島名「提提卡卡」——意為「鉛之岩」。他登上此島,即命太陽、月亮與星辰出現,升入天穹,光照世界——果如其言。相傳月亮初造時比太陽更亮;當二者同時升空之際,太陽心生嫉妒,抓起一把爐灰擲向月亮的面孔——月亮今日那片陰影的顏色,便由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Sun-moon rivalry etiology; tagged with sun-capture for the cluster of solar contests, interpretively.

Viracocha went to this island, and presently ordered that the sun, moon, and stars should come forth, and be set in the heavens to give light to the world, and it was so.

title.en: Taguapaca Bound in the Reed Boat: The Servant Who Preached He Was Viracocha
title.zh: 縛於蘆筏的塔瓜帕卡:自稱維拉科查的僕人

region.zh: 的的喀喀湖(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 7, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: When Viracocha destroyed the first land in the flood he preserved three men - one of them named Taguapaca - that they might serve and help him in the creation of new people in the second age after the deluge. Viracocha gave various orders to his servants, but Taguapaca disobeyed the commands of Viracocha. So Viracocha was enraged against Taguapaca, and ordered the other two servants to take him, tie him hands and feet, and launch him in a balsa on the lake. This was done. Taguapaca was blaspheming against Viracocha for the way he was treated, and threatening that he would return and take vengeance, when he was carried by the water down the drain of the same lake, and was not seen again for a long time. At the end of some years after Viracocha departed, they say that Taguapaca came back and began, with others, to preach that he was Viracocha. Although at first the people were doubtful, they finally saw that it was false, and ridiculed them.
summary.zh: 維拉科查以洪水毀滅初造之地時,留下三名男子助他開創第二次造人——其中一名叫塔瓜帕卡。維拉科查向僕從們發號施令,唯塔瓜帕卡抗命不從。維拉科查大怒,命另外兩名僕人將他手足捆綁,放上蘆葦筏,拋入湖中。塔瓜帕卡一路咒罵維拉科查待他不公,揚言必定回來復仇;湖水將他衝入湖的下泄水道,從此久無蹤影。維拉科查離世數年之後,相傳塔瓜帕卡去而復返,糾集同夥,到處宣講自己就是維拉科查。民眾初時將信將疑,後來識破其偽,群起嘲笑之。

sensitivity.note: The false-preacher servant; Markham's note links Taguapaca/Tarapaca/Tonapa names across sources.

passages.text: Viracocha Pachayachachi, when he destroyed that land as has been already recounted, preserved three men, one of them named Taguapaca, that they might serve and help him in the creation of new people who had to be made in the second age after the deluge. The flood being passed and the land dry, Viracocha determined to people it a second time... Viracocha gave various orders to his servants, but Taguapaca disobeyed the commands of Viracocha. So Viracocha was enraged against Taguapaca, and ordered the other two servants to take him, tie him hands and feet, and launch him in a balsa on the lake. This was done.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 7 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Taguapaca was blaspheming against Viracocha for the way he was treated, and threatening that he would return and take vengeance, when he was carried by the water down the drain of the same lake, and was not seen again for a long time. At the end of some years after Viracocha departed, they say that Taguapaca, who Viracocha ordered to be thrown into the lake of Titicaca in the Collao, came back and began, with others, to preach that he was Viracocha. Although at first the people were doubtful, they finally saw that it was false, and ridiculed them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 7 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

title.en: Fire from Heaven at Cacha: The Hill Burnt Like Straw
title.zh: 卡查天火:焚山如焚稻草

region.zh: 維爾卡馬尤河谷卡查(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 7, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: They tell of a strange event: how Viracocha, after he had created all people, went on his road and came to a place where many men of his creation had congregated - now called Cacha. When Viracocha arrived there, the inhabitants were estranged owing to his dress and bearing; they murmured at it and proposed to kill him from a hill that was near. They took their weapons and gathered together with evil intentions against Viracocha. He, falling on his knees on some plain ground, with his hands clasped, fire from above came down upon those on the hill, and covered all the place, burning up the earth and stones like straw. Those bad men were terrified at the fearful fire; they came down from the hill and sought pardon from Viracocha for their sin. Viracocha was moved by compassion; he went to the flames and put them out with his staff. But the hill remained quite parched up, the stones being rendered so light by the burning that a very large stone which could not have been carried on a cart could be raised easily by one man - a wonderful sight to behold this hill, a quarter of a league in extent, all burnt up.
summary.zh: 相傳維拉科查造畢萬民,沿路而行,至一處民眾聚集之地——即今卡查。居民見其衣冠舉止,心生嫌隙,交相非議,竟謀劃從附近山上將他殺死。他們執持兵器,懷惡意圍聚而來。維拉科查卻在平地上屈膝跪下,合掌向天——頓時天火降於山上那些惡人,火勢席捲全境,大地與石塊如稻草般焚燒。惡徒們被這可怕的天火嚇破膽,下山向維拉科查求赦其罪。維拉科查心生憐憫,走到火場,以杖撲滅火焰。然而山岩已盡被燒枯,石頭燒得極輕——原本牛車都拉不動的巨石,如今一人便可輕易舉起。那片方圓約四分之一萊格、通體焦黑的山巒,至今猶為奇觀。

sensitivity.note: The Cacha temple hill tradition; Markham's note locates it in the Vilcamayu valley and cites the temple described by Squier.

passages.text: They tell of a strange event; how that Viracocha, after he had created all people, went on his road and came to a place where many men of his creation had congregated. This place is now called Cacha. When Viracocha arrived there, the inhabitants were estranged owing to his dress and bearing. They murmured at it and proposed to kill him from a hill that was near. They took their weapons there, and gathered together with evil intentions against Viracocha.

He went to the flames and put them out with his staff. But the hill remained quite parched up, the stones being rendered so light by the burning that a very large stone which could not have been carried on a cart, could be raised easily by one man. This may be seen at this day, and it is a wonderful sight to behold this hill, which is a quarter of a league in extent, all burnt up.

title.en: The Huaca of Urcos and the Golden Bench Taken by Pizarro
title.zh: 烏爾科斯瓦卡與皮薩羅取走的金凳

region.en: Urcos, six leagues south of Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科以南六萊格的烏爾科斯(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 7, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: After this Viracocha continued his journey and arrived at a place called Urcos, six leagues to the south of Cuzco. Remaining there some days he was well served by the natives of that neighbourhood. At the time of his departure, he made them a celebrated huaca or statue, for them to offer gifts to and worship; to which statue the Incas, in after times, offered many rich gifts of gold and other metals, and above all a golden bench. When the Spaniards entered Cuzco they found it, and appropriated it to themselves. It was worth $17,000. The Marquis Don Francisco Pizarro took it himself, as the share of the General.
summary.zh: 其後維拉科查繼續前行,抵達庫斯科以南六萊格的烏爾科斯,在那裡小住數日,備受當地居民款待。臨別之際,他為當地人造了一尊著名的瓦卡神像,供其獻禮崇拜;後世印加王又向此像進獻大量金銀重器,最珍貴的是一張金凳。西班牙人入庫斯科時尋得此凳,據為己有——值一萬七千比索。馬爾基斯·堂弗朗西斯科·皮薩羅以主將之名,親自將它據為己份。

sensitivity.note: The Urcos huaca founded by the Creator-god himself; the loot anecdote ties myth to conquest.

title.en: Walking on the Water Like Foam: The Departure and the Prophecy
title.zh: 踏海如行陸:維拉科查的告別與預言

region.en: Coast at Puerto Viejo and Manta, Ecuador (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 厄瓜多爾老港與曼塔海岸(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 7, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Viracocha continued his journey, working his miracles and instructing his created beings, and reached the territory on the equinoctial line, where are now Puerto Viejo and Manta. Here he was joined by his servants. Intending to leave the land of Peru, he made a speech to those he had created, apprising them of the things that would happen. He told them that people would come who would say that they were Viracocha their creator, and that they were not to believe them; but that in the time to come he would send his messengers who would protect and teach them. Having said this he went to sea with his two servants, and went travelling over the water as if it was land, without sinking; for they appeared like foam over the water, and the people therefore gave them the name of Viracocha, which is the same as to say the grease or foam of the sea.
summary.zh: 維拉科查一面行奇蹟、訓誨所造之民,一面繼續前行,直至赤道之地——即今厄瓜多爾老港與曼塔。兩位僕從在此與他會合。他有意離開秘魯之土,遂向所造之民訓話,告知將來之事:有人會來,自稱是你們的造物主維拉科查——你們不可相信;但將來他必遣使者前來,保護你們、教導你們。言畢,他攜二僕從入海,竟如行陸地一般在水面行走,分毫不沉;他們身影浮於波濤之上,宛如海上泡沫。民眾因此稱他們為「維拉科查」——意即「海之泡沫」。

sensitivity.note: The Creator's prophecy about false Viracochas is read by colonials as foreshadowing the Spaniards; the foam etymology of the name is recorded and disputed by Markham.

title.en: The Sinchis: War Captains of the Age of Liberty
title.zh: 辛奇:自由時代的戰時首領

region.en: Kingdoms of Peru before the Incas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印加之前的秘魯諸邦(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 8, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: From the second creation by Viracocha down to the time of the Incas the land had no regular government: all the people were scattered and disorganized, living in complete liberty, each man being sole lord of his house and estate. In each tribe there were two divisions, Hanansaya (the upper) and Hurinsaya (the lower), a custom which continues to this day. As there were dissensions among them, a certain kind of militia was organized for defence: when it became known that some from other parts were coming to make war, they chose a man known to be a valiant warrior - often such a man offered himself - who was followed and obeyed during the war; when the war was over he became a private man as before, nor did they pay him tribute before or afterwards. To such a man they gave the name of Sinchi, which means valiant. This name of Sinchi for those who held sway only during war lasted throughout the land until the time of Tupac Inca Yupanqui, who instituted Curacas and other officials; even now the custom continues in the provinces of Chile and in the forests east of Quito.
summary.zh: 自維拉科查第二次造人至印加王興起,此地並無常設政權:民眾分散而各自為政,人人得以完全自由,各為自家田宅之主。各族分兩部:上支「哈南薩亞」與下支「烏林薩亞」——此俗沿襲至今。族內不和之時,便組民兵自衛:聞他邦來犯,便擇一名勇士為帥——勇士亦常自薦效力——戰時眾人隨之聽命;戰事一了,帥者復為平民,無論戰前戰後皆不納貢。此等戰將,土人稱之「辛奇」,意即「勇者」。辛奇僅戰時掌權之制,通行全境,直至圖帕克·尤潘琪設「庫拉卡」等官職方廢;今日智利諸省及基多以東森林地帶,戰時唯尊最勇最敢者為首之俗,依然存在。

sensitivity.note: Sarmiento's social-origins chapter: the temporary war-chief as the pre-Inca institution; part of his 'liberty before tyranny' argument.

passages.text: It may be assumed that, although the land was peopled and full of inhabitants before the Incas, it had no regular government, nor did it have natural lords elected by common consent to govern and rule... On the contrary all the people were scattered and disorganized, living in complete liberty, and each man being sole lord of his house and estate. In each tribe there were two divisions. One was called Hanansaya, which means the upper division, and the other Hurinsaya, which is the lower division, a custom which continues to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 8 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: As there were dissensions among them, a certain kind of militia was organized for defence... When it became known to the people of one district that some from other parts were coming to make war, they chose one who was a native, or he might be a stranger, who was known to be a valiant warrior. Often such a man offered himself to aid and to fight for them against their enemies. Such a man was followed and his orders were obeyed during the war. When the war was over he became a private man as he had been before... To such a man they gave and still give the name of Sinchi which means valiant.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 8 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: This name of Sinchi for those who held sway only during war, lasted throughout the land until the time of Tupac Inca Yupanqui, the tenth Inca, who instituted Curacas and other officials... Even at the present time they continue this use and custom in the provinces of Chile and in other parts of the forests of Peru to the east of Quito and Chachapoyas, where they only obey a chief during war time.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 8 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

title.en: Sauaseras, Antasayas and Huallas: The First Tribes of the Cuzco Valley
title.zh: 薩瓦塞拉斯、安塔薩亞斯與瓜利亞斯:庫斯科谷地原住三族

region.zh: 庫斯科谷地(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 9, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: In the valley of Cuzco, owing to its being fertile for cultivation, there were three tribes settled from most ancient times, the first called Sauaseras, the second Antasayas, the third Huallas. They settled near each other, although their lands for sowing were distinct, which is the property they valued most in those days and even now. These natives of the valley lived there in peace for many years, cultivating their farms. Some time before the arrival of the Incas, three Sinchis, strangers to this valley - the first named Alcabisa, the second Copalimayta, and the third Culunchima - collected certain companies and came to the valley of Cuzco, where, by consent of the natives, they settled and became brothers and companions of the original inhabitants. So they lived for a long time. There was concord between these six tribes, three native and three immigrant. They relate that the immigrants came out to where the Incas then resided, as we shall relate presently, and called them relations.
summary.zh: 庫斯科谷地土沃宜耕,自古便有部族定居:第一族名「薩瓦塞拉斯」,第二族名「安塔薩亞斯」,第三族名「瓜利亞斯」。三族毗鄰而居,耕地各自分界——田產乃彼時乃至今日最重之財。谷中土著相安多年,各耕其田。印加人到來之前不久,三位外來辛奇——阿爾卡比薩、科帕利馬伊塔、庫倫奇馬——各聚部眾入谷,徵得土著同意後定居,與原住民結為兄弟同伴,相安甚久。六族之中,土著三族、移民三族,和睦共處。相傳這些移民曾前往印加人當時棲居之地,稱他們為親戚——此點關乎後來的事變。

sensitivity.note: The pre-Inca valley communities - the Alcabisas whom the Incas later claimed as 'relations' to justify dominion.

title.en: Knots and Painted Boards: How the Incas Kept Their Annals
title.zh: 結繩與彩板:印加人的史冊

region.en: Temple of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽神廟(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 9, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: To supply the want of letters these barbarians had a curious invention which was very good and accurate: from fathers to sons they handed down past events, repeating the story of them many times, just as lessons are repeated from a professor's chair, making the hearers say these historical lessons over and over again until they were fixed in the memory; and they recorded on certain cords called quipu, on which they make certain knots by which, and by differences of colour, they distinguish and record each thing as by letters. Besides this they had special historians, an hereditary office descending from father to son. The collection of these annals is due to the great diligence of Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui, the ninth Inca, who sent out a general summons to all the old historians in all the provinces he had subjugated; he had them in Cuzco for a long time, examining them concerning their antiquities, origin, and the most notable events in their history. These were painted on great boards, and deposited in the temple of the Sun, in a great hall. There such boards, adorned with gold, were kept as in our libraries, and learned persons were appointed who were well versed in the art of understanding and declaring their contents. No one was allowed to enter where these boards were kept, except the Inca and the historians, without a special order of the Inca.
summary.zh: 為補無文字之缺,他們有一種極好的記憶之法:父傳子、子傳孫,反覆講述往事,如同師長課徒,令聽者複誦至爛熟於心;又在名為「基普」的繩索上打結,以結形與顏色之別,一一記錄萬事,如以文字書寫。此外還有世襲史官之職,父子相承。這些編年史之集成,端賴第九位印加王帕查庫提·尤潘琪:他傳召所征服諸省的一切老年史官,長期留居庫斯科,考詢其古史源流與要事。所問之事繪於大木板,藏於太陽神廟一大廳之中。這些飾金的彩板,如圖書館藏書般排列;又設通曉釋讀之術的學者。未奉印加王特命,除印加王與史官外,任何人不得入內。

sensitivity.note: The imperial archive of Pachacuti - oral repetition plus quipu cords plus painted boards; Sarmiento's own evidentiary method is described here.

passages.text: The answer is that, to supply the want of letters, these barbarians had a curious invention which was very good and accurate. This was that from one to the other, from fathers to sons, they handed down past events, repeating the story of them many times, just as lessons are repeated from a professor's chair, making the hearers say these historical lessons over and over again until they were fixed in the memory... they recorded, and they still record, the most notable things... on certain cords called quipu... On these cords they make certain knots by which, and by differences of colour, they distinguish and record each thing as by letters.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 9 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.
